glossary.@Published / ObservableObject: Lets a class publish changes so SwiftUI views update.
glossary.@State: View-local state. Changing it re-renders the view.
glossary.Closure ($0): A closure is an inline function. `$0` is the first argument shorthand.
glossary.Force unwrap (!): `!` force-unwraps an optional and crashes if it is nil.
glossary.Optional (?): A `?` means a value might be nil. `??` supplies a default.
glossary.Stacks: Arrange child views vertically, horizontally or layered.
glossary.View / body: A SwiftUI view: a struct whose `body` describes the UI.
glossary.class: A reference type: variables share one instance.
glossary.enum: A fixed set of cases, optionally carrying data.
glossary.extension: Adds functionality to an existing type.
glossary.for-in: Loops over each element of a sequence or range.
glossary.func: Declares a function. `->` gives its return type.
glossary.guard: Checks a condition and must exit the scope in `else` if it fails. Often paired with `let` to unwrap optionals.
glossary.if let: Unwraps an optional; the block runs only when it has a value.
glossary.let: Declares a constant that cannot be reassigned.
glossary.map/filter/reduce: Higher-order functions that transform, select or combine elements using closures.
glossary.protocol: Defines requirements a type can adopt, like an interface.
glossary.struct: A value type: copies are independent. The default way to model data in Swift.
glossary.switch: Matches a value against cases and must be exhaustive.
glossary.var: Declares a variable whose value can change.

lessons.exercise: In a Swift file in Xcode, declare a constant for your name and a variable for your age. Print a sentence using both with interpolation, then try reassigning the constant and read the compiler error.

quiz.explanation: `let` declares a constant. Swift has no `const` keyword.
quiz.prompt: Which keyword declares a value that can never be reassigned?
What type does Swift infer for `let x = 2.5`?

quiz.explanation: Interpolation uses `\(expression)` inside the string. (`+` also works, but option 1 isn't the interpolation form.)

sections.body: `let` creates a constant: once set it never changes. `var` creates a variable you can change later. Prefer `let` by default; Swift will warn you when a `var` is never mutated.
sections.code:
let playerName = "Ada"
var score = 0
score += 10   // fine
// playerName = "Bob"  // error: cannot assign to a let
sections.heading: let vs var

sections.body: Swift works out types from the value you assign. You can also state a type explicitly with a colon.
sections.code:
let lives = 3            // Int
let speed = 2.5          // Double
let title: String = "Quest"
let isAlive = true       // Bool
sections.heading: Type inference

lessons.exercise: Write a function that takes `Int?` and returns the number doubled, or 0 when nil. Do it once with `guard let` and once with `??`.

quiz.explanation: Force-unwrapping nil is a runtime trap. Prefer `if let`, `guard let` or `??`.
quiz.prompt: What happens when you force-unwrap (`!`) a nil optional?

choices: Unwraps y into x for the rest of the scope, or returns
Unwraps only inside an else block
quiz.explanation: `guard let` makes `x` available after the guard and requires the else branch to exit the scope.
quiz.prompt: What does `guard let x = y else { return }` do?

sections.body: A type followed by `?` can hold a value or `nil`. The compiler forces you to deal with the missing case, which prevents a whole class of crashes.
sections.heading: What is an optional?

sections.body: `if let` unwraps for use inside a block. `guard let` unwraps for the rest of the function and exits early otherwise.
sections.heading: if let and guard let

sections.body: `??` supplies a default. `!` force-unwraps and crashes on nil, so avoid it unless you are certain.
sections.heading: Nil-coalescing and force unwrap

quiz.explanation: `-> Type` declares what the function returns.
quiz.prompt: What does `->` in a function declaration introduce?

choices: Removes the argument label at the call site
quiz.explanation: `func f(_ x: Int)` is called as `f(1)` without a label.
quiz.prompt: What does `_` before a parameter name do?

sections.body: Use `func`, list parameters, and give a return type after `->`.
sections.heading: Declaring a function

sections.body: Each parameter has an external label (used by the caller) and an internal name. `_` removes the label. Good labels make call sites read like sentences.
sections.heading: Argument labels

sections.body: Parameters can have defaults, so callers may omit them.
sections.code: func heal(_ amount: Int = 10) -> Int { amount }
sections.heading: Default values

sections.body: Copying a struct copies its data. Structs get a free memberwise initializer and are the default choice in Swift and SwiftUI.
sections.heading: Structs are value types

sections.body: Variables share one instance. Use classes for shared identity, inheritance, or when an API (like ObservableObject) requires it.

sections.body: An array is an ordered list; a dictionary maps keys to values (a lookup returns an optional).
sections.code:
var scores = [10, 20, 30]
scores.append(40)
let levels = ["easy": 1, "hard": 3]
let hard = levels["hard"]   // Int?
sections.heading: Arrays and dictionaries

sections.code:

for i in 0..<3 { print(i) }
